newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Definance banks on multi-media future.
newsitem.headline: Definance banks on multi-media future.

text.p: Belgian holding company Definance SA will spin off non-core activities to focus on pay-television and other media businesses in Belgium and central Europe, a senior executive told Reuters.
But Philippe Lhomme, joint chief executive officer, said the new strategy was unlikely to be reflected in 1996 results.
"The second half of last year was flat and the result will be quite similar to that we had in the middle of last year," he said in an interview. "(1996) was a year of transition."

Definance lost 113 million Belgian francs ($3.34 million) in the six months to June 30, 1996, as 155 million francs of write-downs, mainly on its stake in troubled Antwerp mortgage bank Anhyp, wiped out operating profits.
However, the 13-year-old company was once again confident about its future. "We believe there are no more bad surprises in our portfolio," Lhomme said.
Its focus on media was illustrated by Definance's purchase this month of around 19 percent of Poland's Canal Plus Polska.
The station's other shareholders are French Canal Plus, which holds the 33 percent stake permitted for foreign investors under Polish media law, and local investors.
Definance said it would sell part of its stake on to other local investors, leaving it with around nine percent.
The news of the purchase has helped lift Definance's share to 878 francs from a year low of 702 francs on January 8.

" Canal Plus Polska is doing very well. In the middle of last year there were 70,000 subscribers...I expect it to have reached 150,000 by the end of January," Lhomme said. "We believe Poland could be as successful as Spain for Canal Plus."

Lhomme was looking to invest more in the Czech Republic, where Definance has a 35 percent controlling stake in billboard company EastWest Media. "We are negotiating a deal which will allow it to become the number one in the market," he said.

Definance was studying the Czech television market, at present dominated by TV Nova, a private operator. "When you see a market with such a dominant player there's room for other experiences," Lhomme said.

In Belgium, where Definance already owns about nine percent of Canal Plus Belgium, the company was concentrating on spinning off engineering services company Van Cleemput Industries and real estate fund Immodef by 1998.
Another sale concerns the stake in bank Anhyp, which accounts for 30 to 40 percent of Definance's portfolio. The bank itself had been conducting an 18-month search for a partner.
Lhomme noted Anhyp's shares were at present trading around 5,150 francs, well above the 4,200 franc price at which they were written down in the half year accounts.

The restructuring, once complete, will leave Definance with its 59 percent owned Deficom unit, focusing on media investments, 38 percent of corporate governance specialists Deminor, plus interests in Belgian corporate communications company Decitime and seminar organisers Vanham & Vanham. ($1=33.86 Belgian Franc)
